title: Urban beekeeping and wild bees: hive numbers in Paris and Swiss cities, and competition for flowers

sources.title: Ropars L. et al. (2019) Wild pollinator activity negatively related to honey bee colony densities in urban context. PLOS ONE 14(9): e0222316
Casanelles-Abella J. & Moretti M. (2022) Challenging the sustainability of urban beekeeping using evidence from Swiss cities. npj Urban Sustainability 2, 3
Creating Native Bee Habitat for Gardens in Montana (MontGuide MT202301AG)

facts.text: Paris had about 300 honeybee colonies in 2013 and 687 in 2015, an average of 6.5 colonies per square kilometer.
The Paris density of 6.5 colonies per square kilometer was well above the French national level of 2.5.
From 2014 to 2016, the Paris researchers watched flower patches in city green spaces and recorded 32,694 insect visits to flowers.
Where honeybee colonies nearby were more crowded, wild pollinators visited flowers less often; large solitary bees, beetles and bumblebees were affected.
The effect on large solitary bees and beetles showed within 500 meters of the flowers, and the effect on bumblebees within 1,000 meters.
In Paris, honeybees mostly visited planted garden flowers, while wild pollinators visited planted and wild flowers about equally.
The Paris authors advised against crowding cities with hives and suggested adding flowers and nesting places for wild pollinators instead of more colonies.
In 14 Swiss cities, the number of hives rose from 3,139 in 2012 to 6,370 in 2018, or from 6.48 to 8.1 hives per square kilometer.
The Swiss study found that the cities' green spaces did not offer enough flowers to support that many hives.
Beekeepers do not have to grow flowers for their bees, because honeybees fly freely and feed wherever flowers grow, whoever owns the land.
Large numbers of honeybees can increase competition with wild bees, especially when flowers are scarce.
The Swiss researchers suggested limiting hive numbers, keeping hives apart, and adding flowers and habitat, for example by turning lawns into meadows.
There are an estimated 20,000 bee species in the world, and about 90 percent of them are solitary rather than living in hives.
In a solitary bee species, each female finds or builds her own nest, often in the ground, in hollow stems or in dead wood.
A honeybee colony has a queen and thousands of workers and survives from one year to the next.
Depending on the species, a bee may fly from a few hundred feet to several miles from its nest to find food.
Solitary bees have no honey stores to defend, so they are not aggressive and seldom sting.
A few hundred mason bees can pollinate a fruit orchard as well as thousands of honeybees.
The Swiss authors note that many people see beekeeping as a way to protect nature rather than as a kind of farming.
